title: American Government
description: A survey of the constitutional design, rights, and institutions of the United States government, from the founding debates through today's Congress, presidency, and courts. You will read the Constitution as a working document, trace how federalism divides power, and see how elections, parties, media, and interest groups turn citizen preferences into policy.
outcomes: You can explain how social contract theory and the Declaration of Independence justify limited, consent-based government.
You can describe the Constitution's federalism, separation of powers, and checks and balances with concrete examples of each.
You can distinguish civil liberties from civil rights and trace how landmark cases and laws expanded each.
You can compare the roles of Congress, the presidency, the judiciary, and the bureaucracy in making and enforcing law.
You can analyze how public opinion, parties, interest groups, and media shape elections and policy outcomes.
You can apply the vocabulary of American government to evaluate a real case, election, or policy debate.

units.title: Founding Principles and the Constitution
units.summary: Where the idea of limited government came from, why the first American constitution failed, and how the 1787 Constitution built a durable structure of divided power.

lessons.title: Natural Rights and the Social Contract
lessons.intro: Before there was a Constitution, there was a question: why should anyone obey a government at all? Two English philosophers gave rival answers, and their argument still shapes how Americans talk about rights and rebellion today.

sections.heading: Hobbes, Locke, and the State of Nature
body: Thomas Hobbes imagined life without government, a **state of nature**, as a war of every person against every other, where life was, in his famous phrase, solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short. His fix was a powerful sovereign that people obey absolutely in exchange for protection and order.

John Locke agreed people needed government, but drew a very different lesson. He argued humans have **natural rights** to life, liberty, and property simply by being human, rights that exist before any government and do not depend on a ruler's permission.

For Locke, government is formed by a **social contract**: people consent to be governed only so a neutral authority can protect the rights they already have. Because government exists to serve the people, Locke argued that a government which persistently violates those rights loses its legitimacy and can be replaced.

sections.heading: Locke's Fingerprints on the Declaration of Independence
body: When Thomas Jefferson wrote that all people are endowed with unalienable rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness, he was translating Locke's natural-rights language almost directly, swapping property for the broader pursuit of happiness.

The Declaration also borrows Locke's logic of consent: governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed, and whenever government becomes destructive of these rights, the people have the right to alter or abolish it. That is the social contract, stated as a political argument for independence.

This is why American government is described as **limited government**: the Constitution that followed was designed not to grant rights, which Locke said people already possess, but to restrain government power so those rights stay protected.

example.problem: A colonist in 1776 argues: the king has taxed us without our consent and disbanded our elected assemblies. Using Locke's theory, explain why the colonists believed they were justified in breaking away.
steps: Identify the natural rights at stake: property (taxation without consent) and the right to self-governance (disbanded assemblies).
Apply the social contract: government's only job is to protect natural rights; it has no legitimate power beyond that.
Apply Locke's remedy: when government persistently violates the rights it was created to protect, the people may withdraw consent and form a new government.
example.answer: Because the king violated the terms of the social contract by ignoring the colonists' consent and threatening their rights, Locke's theory holds that the colonists were entitled to dissolve their allegiance and establish new government.

keyTerms.def: A hypothetical condition with no government, used by philosophers to ask why people would agree to be governed at all.
Rights, such as life, liberty, and property, that Locke argued belong to people simply by being human, not granted by government.
The idea that legitimate government arises from the consent of the people, who agree to be governed in exchange for protection of their rights.
A government whose power is restrained by law and constitution so it cannot violate the rights of the people it governs.

practice.q: According to John Locke, where do natural rights come from?
choices: They are granted by a king or sovereign
They belong to people simply by being human, before government exists
They are created by written constitutions
They are earned through military service
practice.explain: Locke argued natural rights such as life, liberty, and property exist prior to government; government's job is to protect them, not grant them.

practice.q: Which phrase in the Declaration of Independence most directly reflects Locke's idea of the social contract?
choices: A more perfect union
Governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed
We hold these truths to be self-evident
Necessary and proper
practice.explain: This phrase states that government's authority comes only from the people's consent, the core of Locke's social contract theory.

practice.q: How did Hobbes's view of the state of nature differ from Locke's?
choices: Hobbes thought the state of nature was peaceful and Locke thought it was violent
Hobbes favored an absolute sovereign for order, while Locke favored limited government to protect pre-existing rights
Hobbes rejected government entirely while Locke supported monarchy
There was no real difference between them
practice.explain: Hobbes wanted a powerful, near-absolute ruler to escape the chaos of the state of nature, while Locke wanted government limited to the job of protecting rights people already had.

lessons.title: From the Articles of Confederation to the Constitution
lessons.intro: America's first national government was so weak it could not put down a rebellion or pay its own debts. Understanding why the Articles of Confederation failed explains almost every design choice made in Philadelphia in 1787.

sections.heading: A Government Too Weak to Govern
body: Fearful of recreating the powerful monarchy they had just fought, the states adopted the **Articles of Confederation** in 1781, creating a loose league of sovereign states with only a single-chamber Congress and no president or national courts.

Congress under the Articles could not tax; it could only request money from the states, who often refused. It could not regulate interstate commerce, so states taxed each other's goods, and it needed the consent of all thirteen states to amend the Articles at all, making reform nearly impossible.

The breaking point was **Shays' Rebellion** in 1786-87, when debt-burdened Massachusetts farmers took up arms to stop foreclosures, and the national government had no army and no money to respond. Nationalists like James Madison and Alexander Hamilton used the crisis to push for a stronger government.

sections.heading: Compromises That Built the Constitution
body: At the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia, large and small states clashed over representation. The **Great Compromise** (Connecticut Compromise) resolved it by creating a bicameral Congress: the House of Representatives apportioned by population, and the Senate with two seats per state regardless of size.

A second dispute pitted Northern and Southern states over whether enslaved people would count toward a state's population, which affected both representation and taxation. The **Three-Fifths Compromise** counted each enslaved person as three-fifths of a person for these calculations, inflating Southern political power while treating enslaved people as property under the law.

A final compromise let Congress regulate interstate and foreign commerce but barred it from taxing exports or banning the international slave trade before 1808. These deals were the price of getting all thirteen states to the table, but they also built lasting injustice into the new government.

example.problem: Under the Articles of Confederation, amending the document required the unanimous consent of all thirteen states. Explain why this rule made the Articles almost impossible to fix, and how the Constitution changed the amendment process.
steps: Under the Articles, a single state could block any change, so reforms that helped twelve states but hurt one state's short-term interest would fail.
This unanimity requirement meant even widely supported fixes, like giving Congress taxing power, repeatedly failed to pass.

The Constitution replaced unanimity with a two-step process: proposal by two-thirds of both houses of Congress (or a national convention), then ratification by three-fourths of the states, letting the document adapt without needing every single state's agreement.
example.answer: The Articles' unanimous-consent rule for amendments gave any one state a veto over reform, which is why the Constitution instead requires two-thirds proposal and three-fourths ratification, a high bar but not an impossible one.

keyTerms.def: The United States' first national constitution (1781-1789), which created a weak central government with no power to tax or regulate commerce.
An armed uprising of indebted Massachusetts farmers in 1786-87 that exposed the national government's inability to respond to internal unrest.
The Constitutional Convention agreement creating a bicameral Congress: a House apportioned by population and a Senate with equal representation per state.
The agreement counting each enslaved person as three-fifths of a person for purposes of representation and taxation.

practice.q: What was the biggest practical weakness of the government under the Articles of Confederation?
choices: It had a president with too much power
Congress could not tax and had no way to enforce laws on the states
The Supreme Court overturned too many laws
States were not allowed to have their own militias
practice.explain: Congress under the Articles could only request funds from states and had no power to tax, regulate commerce, or enforce its own laws, leaving it financially and militarily powerless.

practice.q: The Great Compromise resolved a dispute between which two groups at the Constitutional Convention?
choices: Northern states and Southern states over slavery
Large states and small states over representation in Congress
Federalists and Anti-Federalists over ratification
The states and Britain over trade
practice.explain: Large states wanted representation by population; small states wanted equal representation. The Great Compromise gave both: population-based House, equal Senate.

practice.q: What did the Three-Fifths Compromise do?
choices: Gave enslaved people three-fifths of the right to vote
Freed three-fifths of enslaved people over time
Counted each enslaved person as three-fifths of a person for representation and taxation
Limited slavery to three-fifths of each state's territory
practice.explain: It was a formula for counting population for representation and direct taxes, not a step toward emancipation or voting rights for enslaved people.

lessons.title: Federalism and Separation of Powers
lessons.intro: The Constitution solves the problem of concentrated power twice over: once by splitting authority between national and state governments, and again by splitting the national government itself into three branches that check each other.

sections.heading: Dividing Power Between Nation and States: Federalism
body: **Federalism** divides governing power between a national government and state governments, each sovereign in its own sphere. The Constitution grants the national government **enumerated powers**, such as coining money, declaring war, and regulating interstate commerce, listed mainly in Article I, Section 8.

States keep **reserved powers**, protected by the Tenth Amendment, which states that powers not delegated to the national government nor prohibited to the states belong to the states or the people. This is why states run elections, license drivers, and regulate most schools and police.

Some powers are **concurrent powers**, held by both levels at once, like the power to tax and to build roads. When state and federal law genuinely conflict, the **Supremacy Clause** in Article VI makes federal law the supreme law of the land, so the federal rule wins.

sections.heading: Separation of Powers and Checks and Balances
body: Within the national government, the Constitution assigns lawmaking to Congress (Article I), enforcement to the president (Article II), and interpretation to the courts (Article III). This **separation of powers** prevents any single branch from acting alone across all three functions.

To keep the branches from becoming too powerful even within their own lane, the Constitution layers in **checks and balances**: the president can veto legislation, but Congress can override that veto with a two-thirds vote in both chambers. The Senate must confirm judicial and executive appointments, and courts can strike down laws or executive actions that violate the Constitution.

These checks make American government intentionally slow. A law typically needs House passage, Senate passage, and presidential signature (or a veto override) before it exists, and even then it can later be challenged in court. That friction was deliberate: the framers feared fast, unchecked power more than they feared gridlock.

example.problem: The House and Senate both pass a bill 300-135 and 70-30. The president vetoes it. Does the veto stand, and why?
steps: Overriding a presidential veto requires a two-thirds vote in both the House and the Senate.
Two-thirds of 435 House votes cast (300+135=435) is 290; the House's 300 votes clears that bar.
Two-thirds of the 100 Senate votes cast (70+30=100) is about 66.7; the Senate's 70 votes clears that bar too.
Since both chambers meet the two-thirds threshold, Congress can override the veto and the bill becomes law without the president's signature.
example.answer: No, the veto does not stand: both chambers hit the two-thirds threshold needed to override it, so the bill becomes law over the president's objection.

keyTerms.def: A system that divides governing power between a national government and state governments, each sovereign in its own area.
Powers explicitly granted to the national government by the Constitution, such as coining money and declaring war.
Powers left to the states under the Tenth Amendment, since they are not given to the national government or forbidden to the states.
Dividing government into legislative, executive, and judicial branches so no one branch controls all governmental functions.
Mechanisms, like the veto and veto override, that let each branch limit the power of the other branches.

practice.q: Which power is an example of a power reserved to the states under the Tenth Amendment?
choices: Declaring war
Coining money
Issuing driver's licenses
Regulating interstate commerce
practice.explain: Licensing drivers is not listed as a national power in the Constitution, so under the Tenth Amendment it is reserved to the states.

practice.q: What vote is required in Congress to override a presidential veto?
choices: A simple majority in the House only
Three-fifths in the Senate only
Two-thirds in both the House and the Senate
Unanimous consent in both chambers
practice.explain: Article I requires a two-thirds vote in both the House and the Senate to override a presidential veto and enact the bill into law.

practice.q: If a valid federal law and a state law directly conflict, which wins and why?
choices: The state law, because states have reserved powers
The federal law, because of the Supremacy Clause
Whichever law was passed first
The courts always split the difference
practice.explain: Article VI's Supremacy Clause makes valid federal law supreme over conflicting state law.

units.title: Civil Liberties and Civil Rights
units.summary: The freedoms the Bill of Rights protects from government interference, and the long struggle to extend equal treatment under the law to all Americans.

lessons.title: The Bill of Rights and Freedom of Expression
lessons.intro: Anti-Federalists refused to support the Constitution without an explicit list of protected freedoms. The result, the Bill of Rights, is the reason a government can rarely silence a speaker, ban a religion, or search your home without cause.

sections.heading: Why the Bill of Rights Exists
body: **Civil liberties** are freedoms protected from government interference, like speech, religion, and privacy. The original 1787 Constitution had no bill of rights, and Anti-Federalists like Patrick Henry argued that without one, a strong new national government could trample individual freedom.

Federalists like Hamilton initially argued a bill of rights was unnecessary, and even dangerous, because listing some rights might imply the government could violate any right left off the list. The compromise that secured ratification was a promise to add one immediately, resulting in the first ten amendments, ratified in 1791.

The First Amendment alone protects five distinct freedoms: religion (both the Establishment Clause, barring an official state religion, and the Free Exercise Clause, protecting religious practice), speech, the press, assembly, and petitioning the government.

sections.heading: Limits on Free Speech
body: Free speech is broad but not absolute. The Supreme Court has allowed government to restrict speech that creates a **clear and present danger**, such as falsely shouting fire in a crowded theater, a standard from *Schenck v. United States* (1919) later narrowed to require incitement of imminent lawless action in *Brandenburg v. Ohio* (1969).

Categories like obscenity, defamation (false statements that damage reputation), and true threats also receive little or no First Amendment protection, while political speech, even deeply offensive political speech, receives the strongest protection courts give.

**Symbolic speech**, like flag burning or wearing an armband to protest a war, is generally protected as expressive conduct, as the Court held in *Tinker v. Des Moines* (1969) for students wearing armbands, showing that free expression covers actions as well as words.

example.problem: A city council passes a law banning any public criticism of the mayor. A resident sues, arguing the law violates the First Amendment. Which clause applies, and how would a court likely rule?
steps: Identify the right at stake: this is core political speech, criticism of a government official, which sits at the heart of what the Free Speech Clause protects.
Compare to the narrow categories the Court allows government to restrict: incitement to imminent violence, true threats, obscenity, defamation. Criticism of a mayor fits none of these.
Apply the strong protection given to political speech: laws that punish criticism of officials are classic examples of content-based restrictions that courts strike down.
example.answer: The law almost certainly violates the First Amendment's Free Speech Clause; courts give political criticism of officials the strongest protection and would very likely strike the ban down.

keyTerms.def: Individual freedoms, like speech and religion, protected from government interference.
The first ten amendments to the Constitution, ratified in 1791, protecting specific individual freedoms.
The First Amendment provision barring government from establishing an official religion.
A legal test allowing government to restrict speech that creates an immediate, serious risk of harm.
Expressive conduct, such as flag burning or wearing armbands, protected under the First Amendment as a form of speech.

practice.q: Why did Anti-Federalists insist on adding a Bill of Rights before ratifying the Constitution?
choices: They wanted to abolish the presidency
They feared a strong national government could violate individual freedoms without explicit limits
They wanted states to be able to secede
They believed courts should have no power
practice.explain: Anti-Federalists worried the new, stronger national government created by the Constitution could threaten individual liberty unless specific rights were spelled out and protected.

practice.q: Which type of speech generally receives the LEAST First Amendment protection?
choices: Political criticism of a sitting president
A newspaper editorial opposing a law
True threats of violence against a specific person
A peaceful protest march
practice.explain: True threats fall outside First Amendment protection because they are not expression of ideas but statements intended to instill fear of violence.

practice.q: What did the Supreme Court hold in Tinker v. Des Moines?
choices: Flag burning is illegal
Students wearing armbands to protest were engaged in protected symbolic speech
Schools may ban all student speech
Obscenity is protected speech
practice.explain: Tinker established that non-disruptive symbolic speech, like students wearing armbands, is protected expression under the First Amendment, even in public schools.

lessons.title: Rights of the Accused and the Right to Privacy
lessons.intro: Several amendments protect people the moment they come into contact with police and courts, and the Supreme Court has also found a right to privacy nowhere explicitly written in the constitutional text.

sections.heading: Due Process for the Accused
body: The Fourth Amendment protects against unreasonable searches and seizures, generally requiring police to obtain a warrant based on **probable cause** before searching a home. The **exclusionary rule**, from *Mapp v. Ohio* (1961), bars illegally obtained evidence from being used at trial, giving the Fourth Amendment real teeth.

The Fifth Amendment protects against self-incrimination (the right to remain silent) and double jeopardy (being tried twice for the same crime), and guarantees **due process**, fair legal procedures before government can take life, liberty, or property. *Miranda v. Arizona* (1966) required police to inform suspects of these rights before questioning.

The Sixth Amendment guarantees a speedy public trial by an impartial jury and the right to an attorney; *Gideon v. Wainwright* (1963) held that states must provide a free lawyer to defendants who cannot afford one in serious criminal cases.

example.problem: Police search a suspect's apartment without a warrant or an exception to the warrant requirement, and find evidence of a crime. At trial, the prosecutor wants to use that evidence. What legal rule applies, and what is the likely outcome?
steps: Identify the constitutional violation: a warrantless search without an applicable exception generally violates the Fourth Amendment's protection against unreasonable searches.
Apply the exclusionary rule from Mapp v. Ohio: evidence obtained through an unconstitutional search is generally inadmissible in court.
Conclude the likely outcome: the evidence would probably be suppressed, meaning the prosecutor cannot use it against the defendant at trial.
example.answer: The evidence is likely inadmissible under the exclusionary rule, because it was obtained through a search that violated the Fourth Amendment.

sections.heading: The Right to Privacy
body: The word privacy never appears in the Constitution, but the Supreme Court has found a **right to privacy** implied by several amendments together, including the Third (no quartering soldiers), Fourth (searches), and Fifth (self-incrimination). *Griswold v. Connecticut* (1965) first recognized this right in striking down a law banning contraception for married couples.

The right to privacy became the basis for later, more controversial rulings on reproductive rights, most famously *Roe v. Wade* (1973), which the Court later overturned in *Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization* (2022), returning the question of abortion regulation to the states.

Because the right to privacy rests on inference rather than explicit text, it remains one of the most contested areas of constitutional law, illustrating a bigger theme: many rights Americans take for granted were established by Supreme Court interpretation, not by the Constitution's original words alone.

keyTerms.def: A reasonable basis, more than mere suspicion, for believing a crime has been committed, generally required for a warrant.
The rule barring evidence obtained in violation of the Fourth Amendment from being used at trial.
The constitutional guarantee of fair legal procedures before government can deprive someone of life, liberty, or property.
The warnings, including the right to remain silent and to an attorney, that police must give suspects before custodial interrogation.
A right the Supreme Court has found implied by several amendments, though the word never appears in the Constitution's text.

practice.q: What did Gideon v. Wainwright establish?
choices: Suspects must be read their rights before questioning
States must provide free legal counsel to defendants who cannot afford it in serious cases
Police need a warrant for all searches
Double jeopardy is always permitted
practice.explain: Gideon v. Wainwright held that the Sixth Amendment right to counsel requires states to provide a free attorney to indigent defendants facing serious criminal charges.

practice.q: What does the exclusionary rule do?
choices: It excludes certain people from jury duty
It bars evidence obtained through an unconstitutional search from being used at trial
It excludes hearsay from all trials
It prevents appeals of criminal convictions
practice.explain: Established in Mapp v. Ohio, the exclusionary rule keeps illegally obtained evidence out of court to enforce the Fourth Amendment's protections.

practice.q: Which case first recognized a constitutional right to privacy?
choices: Miranda v. Arizona
Griswold v. Connecticut
Gideon v. Wainwright
Mapp v. Ohio
practice.explain: Griswold v. Connecticut (1965) struck down a law banning contraception for married couples, finding a right to privacy implied by several amendments.

lessons.title: The Struggle for Civil Rights
lessons.intro: Civil liberties protect you from government; civil rights guarantee you equal treatment compared to others. The gap between the Constitution's promises and their enforcement took a civil war, a century of segregation, and a mass movement to begin closing.

sections.heading: Civil Rights vs. Civil Liberties
body: **Civil rights** are protections against discrimination, guaranteeing equal treatment under the law regardless of characteristics like race, sex, or religion. This differs from civil liberties, which limit what government can do to any individual regardless of comparison to others.

The Fourteenth Amendment (1868), ratified after the Civil War, is the constitutional heart of civil rights law. Its **Equal Protection Clause** bars states from denying any person equal protection of the laws, and it also applied most of the Bill of Rights to the states through a process called **incorporation**.

Despite the Fourteenth Amendment, the Supreme Court's *Plessy v. Ferguson* (1896) ruling upheld racial segregation under the doctrine of 'separate but equal,' legalizing Jim Crow segregation across the South for nearly sixty years.

sections.heading: Brown, the Civil Rights Movement, and Landmark Law
body: *Brown v. Board of Education* (1954) unanimously overturned *Plessy*, ruling that segregated public schools were inherently unequal and violated the Equal Protection Clause. Brown gave legal force to a growing movement led by figures like Martin Luther King Jr., Rosa Parks, and countless organizers challenging segregation through boycotts, sit-ins, and marches.

That movement produced the **Civil Rights Act of 1964**, which banned discrimination in employment and public accommodations (restaurants, hotels, theaters) based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin, and the **Voting Rights Act of 1965**, which outlawed discriminatory voting practices like literacy tests and authorized federal oversight of elections in areas with histories of discrimination.

The Supreme Court's *Shelby County v. Holder* (2013) struck down the formula used to decide which areas needed federal preclearance under the Voting Rights Act, and voting rights remain a live and contested area of American politics, showing that civil rights protections require ongoing enforcement, not just a single law or ruling.

example.problem: A state passes a law requiring a specific type of photo ID to vote, and critics argue it disproportionately burdens poorer and minority voters who are less likely to have that ID. Explain what legal framework a court would use to evaluate this law today.
steps: Identify the relevant constitutional and statutory tools: the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment and, if applicable, remaining provisions of the Voting Rights Act.

Note that after Shelby County v. Holder (2013), the preclearance formula is no longer in effect, so the federal government cannot automatically block such laws in previously covered areas before they take effect.

Recognize that challengers would instead need to sue after the law is passed, arguing it has a discriminatory effect or intent under the remaining sections of the Voting Rights Act or the Equal Protection Clause.
example.answer: Because Shelby County v. Holder eliminated automatic federal preclearance, such a law could take effect and would have to be challenged after the fact in court under the Equal Protection Clause or remaining Voting Rights Act provisions, rather than blocked in advance.

keyTerms.def: Legal protections against discrimination that guarantee equal treatment under the law compared to others.
The Fourteenth Amendment provision barring states from denying any person equal protection of the laws.
The process by which the Supreme Court has applied most Bill of Rights protections to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment.
Federal law banning discrimination in employment and public accommodations based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin.
Federal law outlawing discriminatory voting practices and originally requiring federal preclearance of voting changes in certain areas.

practice.q: What is the key difference between civil liberties and civil rights?
choices: Civil liberties apply only to citizens; civil rights apply to everyone
Civil liberties limit government power over any individual; civil rights guarantee equal treatment compared to others
Civil rights come from the Bill of Rights; civil liberties come from the Fourteenth Amendment
There is no meaningful difference
practice.explain: Civil liberties (like free speech) restrain government from certain actions against any person, while civil rights guarantee that people are treated equally to others under the law.

practice.q: What did Brown v. Board of Education (1954) rule?
choices: That segregated schools were constitutional under 'separate but equal'
That segregated public schools violated the Equal Protection Clause
That states could ignore federal civil rights law
That literacy tests for voting were constitutional
practice.explain: Brown v. Board overturned Plessy v. Ferguson's 'separate but equal' doctrine, ruling that segregated public schools were inherently unequal.

practice.q: What was the effect of Shelby County v. Holder (2013)?
choices: It expanded the Voting Rights Act's coverage
It struck down the formula for deciding which areas needed federal preclearance for voting changes
It banned literacy tests for the first time
It overturned Brown v. Board of Education
practice.explain: Shelby County v. Holder invalidated the coverage formula used to require federal preclearance, weakening enforcement of the Voting Rights Act.

units.title: Political Behavior: Opinion, Parties, and Media
units.summary: How Americans form political opinions, how parties and interest groups organize competing coalitions, and how media shapes what voters see and believe.

lessons.title: Public Opinion and Political Ideology
lessons.intro: Politicians and pollsters obsess over public opinion, but a poll is only as good as its sample and its questions. Learning to read polls critically is a basic form of citizen self-defense.

sections.heading: Where Political Opinions Come From
body: **Political socialization** is the lifelong process by which people form political values, shaped by family (the single strongest influence for most people), schools, peers, religion, and media. Most people's basic party attachment forms early and stays fairly stable across their lives.

**Political ideology** describes a consistent set of beliefs about government's proper role. In American politics, **liberal** views typically favor a more active government in the economy and expanded social programs alongside social change, while **conservative** views typically favor limited government economically alongside more traditional social policy, though many voters mix positions across issues.

Ideology is not the same as party identification: many Americans call themselves independents or hold moderate, inconsistent, or issue-specific views that do not map cleanly onto a single left-right scale.

sections.heading: Reading Polls Critically
body: A **public opinion poll** estimates what a whole population thinks by surveying a smaller **sample**. For a poll to be trustworthy, that sample must be randomly selected and large enough to represent the population, and reputable polls report a **margin of error**, the range within which the true value likely falls.

A poll claiming 52% support with a margin of error of plus or minus 4 points really means the true support could be anywhere from 48% to 56%, so a 52-48 lead is statistically too close to call, not a clear result.

Question wording and order can distort results: a leading question that describes a policy favorably will get different answers than a neutral one. Careful readers check who conducted a poll, how the sample was drawn, and the margin of error before trusting a headline number.

example.problem: A poll reports that Candidate A leads Candidate B, 49% to 45%, with a margin of error of ±3 percentage points. Is this a statistically meaningful lead?
steps: Apply the margin of error to each candidate: Candidate A's true support could range from 46% to 52%, and Candidate B's from 42% to 48%.
Check whether the ranges overlap: 46-52 and 42-48 overlap between 46 and 48.
Because the ranges overlap, the race could plausibly be tied or even reversed within the poll's margin of error.
example.answer: No, a 4-point lead with a ±3 margin of error is not a statistically clear lead, because the two candidates' plausible ranges of true support overlap.

keyTerms.def: The lifelong process by which people develop their political values and attachments, shaped by family, school, and media.
A consistent set of beliefs about the proper role and size of government, such as liberal or conservative.
The subset of a population surveyed in a poll, used to estimate the views of the whole population.
The range around a poll's reported result within which the true value likely falls.

practice.q: What is the single strongest influence on most people's early political socialization?
choices: Television advertising
Family
The Supreme Court
Political action committees
practice.explain: Research on political socialization consistently finds family to be the strongest early influence on a person's political values and party attachment.

practice.q: A poll shows 50% support with a margin of error of ±4 points. What is the plausible range of true support?
choices: 50% exactly, no range
practice.explain: Subtracting and adding the 4-point margin of error to the reported 50% gives a plausible range of 46% to 54%.

practice.q: Why do pollsters use a random sample instead of surveying everyone?
choices: Surveying everyone is illegal
A properly drawn random sample can represent the whole population without the cost of surveying everyone
Random samples are always exactly accurate with no error
It is required by the Constitution
practice.explain: A well-designed random sample lets pollsters estimate the views of a large population efficiently, though it still carries some margin of error.

lessons.title: Political Parties and the Two-Party System
lessons.intro: The Constitution never mentions political parties, yet American politics has been organized around two dominant parties for most of its history. Understanding why reveals a lot about how U.S. elections actually work.

sections.heading: What Parties Do
body: A **political party** is an organization that recruits, nominates, and helps elect candidates who share a broad label and set of priorities. Parties perform key functions: simplifying choices for voters, organizing government (committee assignments, legislative leadership), and holding officials accountable at the next election.

The modern Democratic and Republican parties trace to the mid-1800s; Democrats generally favor more active government involvement in the economy and social programs, while Republicans generally favor lower taxes, less regulation, and more limited federal government, though both parties contain internal factions and have shifted positions over time.

**Party platforms**, adopted at national conventions, state each party's official positions, though individual candidates often diverge from the platform on specific issues to fit their district or state.

sections.heading: Why Two Parties Dominate
body: The United States' **single-member district, winner-take-all** electoral system (also called first-past-the-post) tends to produce two dominant parties, a pattern political scientists call **Duverger's Law**: when only one candidate per district can win, voters and donors gravitate toward the two parties seen as viable, starving smaller parties of support.

Ballot access laws, the structure of the Electoral College, and campaign finance systems built around two major parties further reinforce this pattern, making it very difficult for third parties to win seats even when they attract meaningful vote shares.

**Third parties** still matter, though: they can act as a safety valve for frustrated voters, push issues (like the environment or trade) onto the major parties' agendas, and occasionally act as **spoilers**, drawing enough votes from one major party to change which major-party candidate wins.

example.problem: In a hypothetical presidential race, Candidate A gets 48% of the vote, Candidate B gets 47%, and a third-party Candidate C gets 5%. Exit polls suggest most of Candidate C's voters would have picked Candidate B if C had not run. Explain the 'spoiler effect' at work here.
steps: Note the outcome without Candidate C: Candidate A wins with a plurality (48% to 47%).
Consider where Candidate C's 5% would likely have gone: mostly to Candidate B, based on the exit poll data.
Recompute the likely two-way result: Candidate B would gain most of that 5%, potentially pushing B above A's 48%, reversing the outcome.
example.answer: Candidate C acted as a spoiler: by drawing votes that would likely have gone to Candidate B, C's candidacy may have changed the winner from B to A, even without C coming close to winning.

keyTerms.def: An organization that recruits, nominates, and helps elect candidates who share a common label and policy priorities.
The official statement of a party's positions on issues, adopted at its national convention.
The observation that winner-take-all, single-member district elections tend to produce two dominant parties.
When a third-party or independent candidate draws enough votes from one major-party candidate to change the election's outcome.

practice.q: Why does Duverger's Law predict a two-party system in the United States?
choices: The Constitution requires exactly two parties
Winner-take-all, single-member district elections push voters and donors toward the two parties seen as able to win
Third parties are illegal
The Supreme Court banned multi-party systems
practice.explain: In winner-take-all elections, votes for a party unlikely to win a given district feel wasted, so support consolidates around the two most viable parties over time.

practice.q: What is a 'spoiler effect' in an election?
choices: When a candidate wins by a landslide
When a third-party candidate draws votes that change which major-party candidate wins
When a poll is conducted incorrectly
When a candidate withdraws before an election
practice.explain: A spoiler effect occurs when a minor candidate pulls enough votes from one major candidate to flip the result to the other major candidate.

practice.q: Which of these is a core function political parties perform in American government?
choices: Writing the Constitution
Simplifying voter choices and organizing government, such as committee assignments
Serving as one of the three constitutional branches
Appointing federal judges directly
practice.explain: Parties are not a constitutional branch of government; their role is to organize candidates, simplify choices for voters, and structure legislative organization like committees and leadership.

lessons.title: Interest Groups and the Media
lessons.intro: Between elections, most political influence flows through organized interest groups and the media that covers them. Both shape policy in ways most citizens never fully see.

sections.heading: Interest Groups and Lobbying
body: An **interest group** is an organization of people sharing a common goal who try to influence public policy, from the National Rifle Association to labor unions to the American Association of Retired Persons. Unlike parties, interest groups do not run their own candidates for office; they try to influence whoever holds office.

**Lobbying** is the direct effort to persuade lawmakers or regulators, done by professional lobbyists who provide research, draft bill language, and testify at hearings. Groups also mobilize members to contact officials and run public advertising campaigns to shape opinion before a vote.

**Political action committees (PACs)** raise and spend money to support or oppose candidates. Federal law limits how much a PAC can donate directly to a candidate, but **super PACs**, created after the *Citizens United v. FEC* (2010) ruling, can raise and spend unlimited amounts on ads, as long as they do not coordinate directly with a candidate's campaign.

sections.heading: The Media's Role in Politics
body: The media informs voters, but it also shapes politics through **agenda-setting**, the power to influence which issues the public sees as important simply by choosing what to cover heavily, even without telling people what to think about those issues.

**Framing** describes how a story is presented, which can shift public reaction even when the underlying facts are the same: describing a policy as 'tax relief' versus 'tax cuts for the wealthy' can produce very different public responses to identical numbers.

The rise of cable news, talk radio, and social media has fragmented the media landscape, letting people select sources that match their existing views, a pattern called **selective exposure**, which researchers link to rising political polarization since audiences increasingly consume different facts and framing depending on their political identity.

example.problem: Two news outlets cover the same new law that raises the minimum wage. Outlet 1's headline reads 'Lawmakers Raise Pay for Millions of Workers.' Outlet 2's headline reads 'New Mandate Forces Small Businesses to Cut Jobs.' Explain what media effect is at work, and why it matters even though both headlines could be factually defensible.
steps: Identify that both outlets are covering the identical underlying event: a minimum wage increase.
Recognize the difference is in emphasis and word choice, not necessarily fabricated facts: this is the definition of framing.
Explain the consequence: readers exposed only to one frame will form very different impressions of the same policy, reinforcing whatever view their chosen outlet already holds.
example.answer: This is framing: both outlets choose which true aspects of the story to emphasize, shaping public perception of the same policy in opposite directions without necessarily reporting anything false.

keyTerms.def: An organization of people sharing a common goal that tries to influence public policy without running its own candidates.
Direct efforts to persuade lawmakers or regulators to support or oppose specific policies.
A political committee that can raise and spend unlimited money on election ads, as long as it does not coordinate directly with a candidate's campaign.
The media's power to influence which issues the public sees as important through the choice of what to cover.
How a story is presented, including word choice and emphasis, which can shape public reaction to the same underlying facts.

practice.q: What is the key difference between a political party and an interest group?
choices: Interest groups run their own candidates for office; parties do not
Parties try to win elections with their own candidates; interest groups try to influence whoever is in office
Interest groups are illegal; parties are not
There is no meaningful difference
practice.explain: Parties nominate and elect their own candidates under a shared label; interest groups instead try to influence officials from outside, regardless of party.

practice.q: What did Citizens United v. FEC (2010) enable?
choices: Unlimited direct donations to candidates
The creation of super PACs that can raise and spend unlimited money as long as they do not coordinate with a campaign
A ban on all campaign advertising
Direct public financing of all elections
practice.explain: Citizens United allowed unlimited independent political spending by groups like super PACs, though direct coordination with candidates and direct-donation limits remain restricted.

practice.q: Describing a policy as 'tax relief' rather than 'a tax cut for the wealthy' to shift public reaction is an example of:
choices: Agenda-setting
Framing
Lobbying
Political socialization
practice.explain: This is framing: presenting the same underlying fact using language chosen to produce a particular emotional or political reaction.

units.title: The National Institutions
units.summary: How Congress, the presidency, the judiciary, and the federal bureaucracy actually make, enforce, and interpret law day to day.

lessons.title: Congress: Structure and Lawmaking
lessons.intro: Congress is the branch closest to the people, elected directly and most often blamed for gridlock. Seeing how a bill actually becomes law explains why change in Washington is usually slow and hard-won.

sections.heading: A Bicameral Congress
body: Congress has two chambers. The **House of Representatives** has 435 members serving two-year terms, apportioned among states by population and reapportioned after each census; California, the most populous state, has far more House seats than sparsely populated states like Wyoming.

The **Senate** has 100 members, two per state regardless of population, serving staggered six-year terms so about a third of the Senate is up for election every two years. This gives smaller states outsized influence per capita in the Senate compared to the House.

Both chambers rely heavily on **committees** to do the real work of writing and vetting legislation; a bill is typically assigned to a relevant committee, such as Armed Services or Ways and Means, which can amend, approve, or simply ignore it, killing most bills before they ever reach a floor vote.

sections.heading: How a Bill Becomes Law
body: A bill must pass both the House and Senate in identical form, then go to the president. If the House and Senate pass different versions, a **conference committee** works out a compromise version that both chambers must then approve again before it goes to the president.

The Senate has a distinctive tool unavailable in the House: the **filibuster**, extended debate that can delay a vote indefinitely unless 60 senators vote for **cloture** to end debate. This effectively means many bills need 60 votes in the Senate, not a simple majority, to pass.

Once passed by both chambers, the president can sign the bill into law, veto it (sending it back to Congress, which can override with two-thirds votes in both chambers), or take no action; if Congress is in session, the bill becomes law after ten days without a signature, but if Congress adjourns during that window, it dies through a **pocket veto**.

example.problem: A bill has 55 votes in favor in the Senate, and a minority opposes it and refuses to end debate. Can the bill pass?
steps: Recognize that ending a filibuster requires a cloture vote of 60 senators, not the 51 needed for a simple majority.
Compare: the bill has 55 supporters, below the 60 needed for cloture.
Conclude that without 5 more votes for cloture, the minority can block a final vote indefinitely, even though a majority supports the bill.
example.answer: No, with only 55 votes the bill cannot overcome a filibuster, since ending debate requires 60 votes for cloture; the bill would be blocked unless supporters find 5 more votes or use a special process like reconciliation.

keyTerms.def: The 435-member chamber of Congress apportioned by state population, with members serving two-year terms.
The 100-member chamber of Congress with two senators per state, serving staggered six-year terms.
Extended Senate debate used to delay or block a vote, which can only be ended by a 60-vote cloture motion.
A temporary committee of House and Senate members that reconciles differing versions of a bill.
The death of a bill when the president does not sign it and Congress adjourns within the ten-day signing window.

practice.q: Why can smaller states have outsized influence in the Senate compared to the House?
choices: Senators serve shorter terms than representatives
Every state gets two senators regardless of population, while House seats are apportioned by population
Senators are appointed, not elected
Small states get extra House seats too
practice.explain: Because every state, regardless of size, gets exactly two senators, a small state's residents have far more Senate representation per capita than a large state's residents.

practice.q: What is needed to end a Senate filibuster?
choices: A simple majority of 51 votes
A cloture vote of 60 senators
Unanimous consent of all 100 senators
A presidential order
practice.explain: Ending debate on most legislation in the Senate requires a cloture vote supported by 60 senators, well above a simple majority.

practice.q: What happens if the House and Senate pass different versions of the same bill?
choices: The bill automatically fails
A conference committee works out a compromise version both chambers must approve
The president chooses which version to sign
The Supreme Court decides
practice.explain: A conference committee, made up of members from both chambers, negotiates a single compromise bill that the House and Senate must both pass again before it can go to the president.

lessons.title: The Presidency and Executive Power
lessons.intro: The Constitution's description of presidential power fits in a few paragraphs, yet the modern presidency touches nearly every part of American life. Much of that power was built through practice, not just text.

sections.heading: Formal Powers of the President
body: Article II grants the president **formal powers**: commander in chief of the armed forces, the power to make treaties (with two-thirds Senate approval), to appoint federal judges and executive officials (with Senate confirmation), to grant pardons for federal crimes, and to veto legislation.

The president also delivers the annual **State of the Union** address and can call Congress into special session, giving the office influence over Congress's agenda even without a formal vote in the legislative process.

Presidential appointments are extensive: the president nominates cabinet secretaries, federal judges (including Supreme Court justices), and thousands of other executive officials, though nearly all major appointments require Senate confirmation, a significant check on unilateral presidential power.

sections.heading: Informal and Expanding Executive Power
body: Beyond the Constitution's text, presidents have built **informal powers** through practice. An **executive order** directs federal agencies on how to implement existing law, without needing congressional approval; it can be significant, but the next president can typically reverse it, and courts can strike one down if it exceeds legal authority.

Presidents also negotiate **executive agreements** with foreign countries, which function like treaties but do not require Senate ratification, letting presidents conduct much foreign policy without formal Senate involvement.

The modern presidency's growth is also driven by the **bully pulpit**, the president's unmatched platform to shape public opinion and pressure Congress, and by crises and wars, during which Congress and courts have historically deferred more power to the executive.

example.problem: A president issues an executive order directing an agency to stop enforcing a certain regulation. A new president takes office two years later and disagrees with that order. What can the new president do, and what limits apply?
steps: Recognize that executive orders direct how existing law is implemented but do not themselves have the permanence of a statute passed by Congress.
Apply the rule that a sitting president can issue a new executive order reversing or modifying a prior president's order, since both derive from the same executive authority.
Note the limits: the new order still cannot exceed the president's legal authority, cannot contradict a statute Congress has passed, and can still be challenged in court.
example.answer: The new president can issue a new executive order reversing the prior one, since executive orders are not permanent law; but like any executive order, it remains subject to legal limits and judicial review.

keyTerms.def: The president's constitutional role as head of the U.S. armed forces.
A presidential directive to federal agencies on how to implement existing law, issued without congressional approval.
An international agreement made by the president that functions like a treaty but does not require Senate ratification.
The president's platform and visibility, used to shape public opinion and pressure Congress.

practice.q: Which of these presidential powers requires Senate approval?
choices: Issuing an executive order
Ratifying a treaty
Delivering the State of the Union address
Using the bully pulpit
practice.explain: Treaties require approval by two-thirds of the Senate to be ratified; executive orders, the State of the Union, and the bully pulpit do not require Senate approval.

practice.q: How do executive agreements differ from treaties?
choices: Executive agreements require a two-thirds Senate vote; treaties do not
Executive agreements function like treaties but do not require Senate ratification
Executive agreements only apply to domestic policy
There is no real difference
practice.explain: Executive agreements let the president make binding international arrangements without going through the formal Senate treaty-ratification process.

practice.q: Can a sitting president reverse a previous president's executive order?
choices: No, executive orders are permanent once issued
Yes, a new executive order can reverse or modify a prior one, subject to legal limits
Only Congress can undo an executive order
Only the Supreme Court can undo an executive order
practice.explain: Executive orders are not statutes; a sitting president can issue a new order reversing a predecessor's, as long as it still fits within legal authority.

lessons.title: The Judiciary and the Bureaucracy
lessons.intro: Unelected judges can strike down laws passed by elected legislatures, and an enormous federal bureaucracy writes and enforces rules that touch daily life far more than most acts of Congress. Neither power is obvious from a first reading of the Constitution.

sections.heading: Judicial Review and the Federal Courts
body: The federal judiciary has three main levels: district courts (trial courts), circuit courts of appeals (which review district court decisions), and the Supreme Court, the final court of appeal, with nine justices who serve for life during good behavior.

The power of **judicial review**, the authority of courts to strike down laws or executive actions that violate the Constitution, is not explicitly stated in the Constitution. The Supreme Court claimed this power for itself in *Marbury v. Madison* (1803), when Chief Justice John Marshall ruled that a section of a federal law conflicted with the Constitution and was therefore void.

Judicial review makes the Supreme Court an enormously powerful check on the other branches, since its constitutional interpretations are binding unless overturned by a later Court decision or a formal constitutional amendment, which requires the difficult two-thirds-and-three-fourths process.

example.problem: Congress passes a law, and a lower federal court strikes it down as unconstitutional. The federal government appeals all the way to the Supreme Court, which rules 6-3 that the law is constitutional after all. What happens to the law, and why does this show the power of judicial review?
steps: Recognize that lower federal courts can rule on constitutionality, but the Supreme Court has final say as the highest court in the judicial hierarchy.
Apply the Supreme Court's ruling: since it upheld the law 6-3, the law stands and takes effect, overriding the lower court's decision.

Connect this to judicial review: the power to make this final call over an elected Congress's law belongs to unelected, life-tenured justices, showing how much authority judicial review gives the judiciary.
example.answer: The law stands, because the Supreme Court's ruling is the final word in the judicial system; this illustrates judicial review's power, since nine unelected justices can have the final say on whether an elected Congress's law is constitutional.

sections.heading: The Federal Bureaucracy
body: The **federal bureaucracy** consists of the executive departments (like State, Defense, and Education), independent agencies (like the Environmental Protection Agency), and government corporations that implement and enforce law on a daily basis. Congress passes broad statutes, and agencies fill in the details through **rulemaking**.

This delegation happens because Congress cannot write detailed technical rules for every possible situation; instead, it grants agencies authority to create specific regulations within the boundaries Congress sets, subject to notice-and-comment procedures that let the public weigh in before a rule is finalized.

Bureaucratic agencies are led by political appointees but staffed mostly by career **civil servants**, protected from being fired for political reasons by civil service laws passed after the Pendleton Act of 1883 ended the old **spoils system**, in which government jobs were handed out as rewards for political loyalty rather than merit.

keyTerms.def: The power of courts to strike down laws or executive actions that violate the Constitution, established in Marbury v. Madison.
The 1803 Supreme Court case that established the power of judicial review.
The departments, agencies, and government corporations that implement and enforce laws passed by Congress.
The process by which federal agencies create specific, detailed regulations within authority granted by Congress.
The historical practice of awarding government jobs based on political loyalty rather than merit, largely ended by the Pendleton Act of 1883.

practice.q: What did Marbury v. Madison (1803) establish?
choices: The right to a jury trial
The power of judicial review
The spoils system
The filibuster
practice.explain: Marbury v. Madison established that federal courts have the power to strike down laws that conflict with the Constitution, a power not explicitly stated in the Constitution's text.

practice.q: Why does Congress delegate rulemaking authority to federal agencies?
choices: The Constitution requires it explicitly
Congress cannot write detailed technical rules for every situation, so agencies fill in specifics within limits Congress sets
Agencies have more votes than Congress
It is a temporary emergency power only
practice.explain: Because Congress cannot anticipate every technical detail, it passes broader statutes and lets expert agencies create specific regulations within the boundaries it sets.

practice.q: What did the Pendleton Act of 1883 do?
choices: Created the federal income tax
Began replacing the spoils system with a merit-based civil service
Established judicial review
Created the Federal Reserve
practice.explain: The Pendleton Act began requiring competitive exams and merit-based hiring for federal jobs, reducing the practice of awarding jobs purely for political loyalty.

units.title: Elections, Federalism in Practice, and Civic Life
units.summary: How presidential elections actually get decided, how power plays out between national, state, and local governments, and how citizens engage with the system beyond voting.

lessons.title: The Electoral College and Elections
lessons.intro: Americans do not directly elect their president. A separate system, the Electoral College, decides the outcome, and it has produced a president who lost the popular vote five times in U.S. history.

sections.heading: How the Electoral College Works
body: Each state gets a number of **electors** equal to its total representation in Congress (House seats plus two senators), and Washington, D.C. gets three electors under the Twenty-Third Amendment, for 538 electors total. A candidate needs a majority, 270 electoral votes, to win the presidency.

In every state except Maine and Nebraska, the candidate who wins the statewide popular vote receives all of that state's electoral votes, a winner-take-all system. This means a candidate can win the national popular vote yet lose the Electoral College, as happened in 2000 and 2016, if their support is inefficiently distributed across states.

If no candidate reaches 270 votes, the Twelfth Amendment sends the decision to the House of Representatives, where each state delegation casts a single vote, regardless of the state's population; this has happened only once, in 1824.

example.problem: A candidate wins California (54 electoral votes), Texas (40), Florida (30), and New York (28), along with enough smaller states to reach exactly 270 electoral votes total. Has this candidate won the presidency, even if they received fewer total popular votes nationwide than their opponent?
steps: Recall the constitutional rule: winning the presidency requires 270 electoral votes, not a majority of the national popular vote.
Confirm the candidate has reached exactly 270, the threshold for an outright majority of the 538 electors.
Apply the historical precedent (2000, 2016): a candidate can reach 270 electoral votes while losing the national popular vote, and the Electoral College result is what determines the winner.
example.answer: Yes, reaching 270 electoral votes wins the presidency under the Constitution, regardless of the national popular vote total, exactly as happened in 2000 and 2016.

sections.heading: Primaries, Turnout, and Redistricting
body: Before the general election, parties select nominees through **primaries** (elections run by the state, where voters directly choose a candidate) or **caucuses** (local meetings where party members debate and vote), with rules on who can participate varying widely by state and party.

**Voter turnout** in the U.S. is lower than in many other democracies, especially in midterm and local elections; barriers like registration deadlines, voter ID laws, and limited polling access all affect how many eligible citizens actually vote, alongside simple factors like interest and a sense that one's vote matters.

Every ten years, after the census, House districts are redrawn to reflect population changes, a process called **redistricting**. When the party in power draws district lines to maximize its own seats, this is called **gerrymandering**, and it remains legal for partisan advantage in most states even though courts have struck down maps drawn to dilute votes based on race.

keyTerms.def: The body of 538 electors, apportioned by state, whose votes formally decide the presidency; 270 votes are needed to win.
The system, used in nearly every state, in which the candidate winning the statewide popular vote receives all of that state's electoral votes.
A state-run election in which voters choose a party's nominee for the general election.
The process of redrawing legislative district boundaries after each census to reflect population changes.
Drawing legislative district lines to give one political party an advantage.

practice.q: How many electoral votes are needed to win the presidency?
practice.explain: There are 538 total electors, and a candidate needs a majority, 270, to win the presidency outright.

practice.q: What happens in most states under the winner-take-all electoral system?
choices: Electoral votes are split proportionally to the popular vote
The candidate winning the statewide popular vote gets all of that state's electoral votes
The state legislature chooses the electors directly regardless of the vote
Electoral votes go to the national popular vote winner
practice.explain: In every state except Maine and Nebraska, whichever candidate wins the state's popular vote receives all of that state's electoral votes.

practice.q: What is gerrymandering?
choices: Requiring photo ID to vote
Drawing legislative district lines to benefit one political party
Counting votes after a recount
Running a caucus instead of a primary
practice.explain: Gerrymandering is the practice of drawing district boundaries specifically to favor one party's chances of winning seats.

lessons.title: State and Local Government
lessons.intro: Most of the government decisions that touch daily life, from school policy to garbage collection to speed limits, come from state and local governments, not Washington.

sections.heading: State Governments
body: Every state has its own constitution, typically much longer and more detailed than the federal Constitution, and its own three branches: a governor (executive), a state legislature (nearly always bicameral except Nebraska's unicameral legislature), and state courts, which handle the vast majority of the nation's legal cases.

States hold broad **police power**, the authority to regulate for public health, safety, welfare, and morals, which is why marriage law, most criminal law, education standards, and professional licensing are set mainly at the state level rather than federally.

Federal grants, especially **categorical grants** (for specific purposes, with conditions attached) and **block grants** (for broader purposes, with more state discretion), give the national government leverage over state policy even in areas it cannot directly control, since states risk losing funding if they refuse the attached conditions.

sections.heading: Local Government and Civic Engagement
body: **Local governments**, including counties, cities, towns, and special districts (like school boards or water districts), are created by state law and exercise only the powers their state constitution or legislature grants them, a principle summarized by **Dillon's Rule** in many states, versus **home rule**, which gives some cities broader independent authority.

Citizens engage with government far beyond voting: contacting elected officials, attending public hearings, serving on juries, joining advocacy groups, protesting, and running for local office (like school board) are all common, often lower-barrier forms of participation.

Local elections typically have much lower turnout than presidential elections, even though local officials often make decisions, like property taxes, zoning, and school budgets, with more direct daily impact on residents than most federal policy.

example.problem: A city council wants to pass a stricter environmental ordinance than state law requires. Under a home rule system, can it do so? Under Dillon's Rule, could it?
steps: Recall that home rule gives cities broad independent authority to legislate on local matters unless state law specifically forbids it.
Recall that under Dillon's Rule, a local government can only exercise powers explicitly granted to it (or clearly implied) by the state.

Compare: under home rule, the city likely can pass the stricter ordinance unless state law preempts it; under Dillon's Rule, the city would need to point to specific state authorization for that kind of ordinance, or it may be blocked.
example.answer: Under home rule, the city likely can pass the stricter ordinance on its own authority; under Dillon's Rule, it would need explicit state authorization, and without it the ordinance could be challenged as beyond the city's granted powers.

keyTerms.def: The broad authority of states to regulate for public health, safety, welfare, and morals.
Federal funding given to states for a specific purpose, with conditions attached.
Federal funding given to states for a broader purpose, with more discretion over how to spend it.
The legal principle that local governments only have the powers explicitly granted to them by the state.
A system giving cities broader independent authority to govern local matters without specific state authorization for each action.

practice.q: What is the 'police power' of state governments?
choices: The authority to run local police departments only
The broad authority to regulate for public health, safety, welfare, and morals
A power only the federal government holds
The power to declare war
practice.explain: Police power is the states' broad regulatory authority over health, safety, welfare, and morals, which is why most criminal law and licensing happens at the state level.

practice.q: What is the key difference between a categorical grant and a block grant?
choices: Categorical grants are for a specific purpose with conditions; block grants are broader with more state discretion
Block grants always come with more federal conditions than categorical grants
Categorical grants go only to local governments
There is no real difference
practice.explain: Categorical grants target specific purposes and attach conditions, while block grants fund a broader area and give states more flexibility in how to use the money.

practice.q: Under Dillon's Rule, what powers can a local government exercise?
choices: Any power not explicitly forbidden by the state
Only powers explicitly granted (or clearly implied) by the state
Unlimited powers, same as the state itself
Only powers granted by the federal government
practice.explain: Dillon's Rule limits local governments to powers the state has explicitly given them, unlike home rule, which presumes broader local authority.

lessons.title: Foreign Policy and Civic Engagement
lessons.intro: Foreign policy is one area where the Constitution deliberately splits power between Congress and the president, forcing them to cooperate even when they disagree, and it is also where individual civic engagement can feel most distant, yet still matters.

sections.heading: Making Foreign Policy
body: The Constitution divides foreign policy power: the president negotiates treaties and serves as commander in chief, but the Senate must ratify treaties by a two-thirds vote, and only Congress holds the constitutional power to formally **declare war**, a power Congress has exercised only a handful of times, most recently in World War II.

In practice, presidents have sent U.S. forces into extended conflict without a formal declaration of war, often citing existing authorizations or their role as commander in chief. The **War Powers Resolution** of 1973 requires presidents to notify Congress within 48 hours of committing forces and limits deployments to 60 days without congressional approval, though presidents have disputed its constitutionality and its enforcement has been inconsistent.

Foreign policy tools beyond military force include diplomacy (negotiation through the State Department and ambassadors), economic sanctions (restricting trade or financial transactions to pressure another country), and foreign aid, all used to influence other nations without direct military conflict.

sections.heading: Civic Engagement Beyond Voting
body: **Civic engagement** includes far more than casting a ballot every few years: contacting representatives, testifying at public hearings, serving on a jury, volunteering for campaigns, joining or organizing advocacy groups, and peaceful protest are all constitutionally protected and historically significant forms of participation.

**Political efficacy**, a citizen's belief that their participation can actually make a difference, strongly predicts whether people engage at all; when people believe government does not listen, participation tends to drop, which can become self-reinforcing.

Understanding the system covered in this course, how a bill becomes law, how courts interpret rights, how elections are decided, is itself a form of civic capacity: it lets you identify where in the system to apply pressure on an issue you care about, rather than treating government as an unreadable black box.

example.problem: A president deploys troops abroad without a formal declaration of war, citing commander-in-chief authority. Sixty-five days pass with troops still deployed and no congressional authorization. According to the War Powers Resolution, what is supposed to happen, and what makes this framework hard to enforce in practice?
steps: Recall the War Powers Resolution's rule: the president must notify Congress within 48 hours and end deployment within 60 days without congressional approval (plus a 30-day withdrawal window).
Apply the timeline: at 65 days without authorization, the president is technically past the deadline set by the resolution.

Note the enforcement problem: presidents of both parties have argued the resolution unconstitutionally limits their commander-in-chief power, and Congress has rarely forced compliance through its own tools, like cutting off funding.
example.answer: Under the War Powers Resolution, the deployment should have ended by day 60 (or 90 with the withdrawal window) without congressional authorization; in practice, the resolution is weakly enforced because presidents dispute its constitutionality and Congress has rarely used its power of the purse to force a withdrawal.

keyTerms.def: The constitutional power, held solely by Congress, to formally declare a state of war.
A 1973 law requiring presidents to notify Congress within 48 hours of deploying forces and limiting deployment to 60 days without congressional approval.
Restrictions on trade or financial transactions used to pressure another country's government or policies.
Participation in public life beyond voting, including contacting officials, protesting, and joining advocacy groups.
A citizen's belief that their political participation can actually make a difference.

practice.q: Which branch of government holds the constitutional power to formally declare war?
choices: The president alone
Congress
The Supreme Court
State governments
practice.explain: Article I gives Congress, not the president, the power to declare war, though presidents as commander in chief have often deployed forces without a formal declaration.

practice.q: What does the War Powers Resolution of 1973 require?
choices: Congress must approve every military exercise in advance
The president must notify Congress within 48 hours of deploying forces and generally end deployment within 60 days without approval
The president can never deploy troops without a declared war
States must approve federal military deployments
practice.explain: The War Powers Resolution sets notification and time limits on presidential deployments without congressional authorization, though its enforcement has been inconsistent.

practice.q: What does 'political efficacy' refer to?
choices: A politician's success rate in elections
A citizen's belief that their participation can make a difference
